speaker_name: A white cord in the swallet's throat
notes: The Hound's Swallet's hook post (world/sites/site_exterior.gd _hook). Lore; the quest is Tamsin Hounder's at the Scourers' Lodge.

look.speaker: A white cord in the swallet's throat
look.text: A scourer's white cord, the kind the Hounders tie on their lodge gate after every scouring, runs from a stake here down over the lip of the swallet and into the dark. It is tied to a rake-head wedged in the rock, and when you put a hand on it it is taut, as if something a long way down were lying on the other end. Wolf-hair is caught in the knot, grey-gold, and one white hair as long as your forearm.

pluck.speaker: A white cord in the swallet's throat
pluck.text: It hums like a bowstring, a long way down, and stops, as if a hand had closed on it. From somewhere under the down something breathes out.

speaker_name: The cords on the lodge gate
notes: A touch on the Scourers' Lodge gate (hearthvale.gd scourers_lodge).

look.speaker: The cords on the lodge gate
look.text: Seventy-one white cords knotted along the top bar of the gate, one for every scouring of the Chalk Hound. The oldest are grey and furred with lichen; the newest is seven summers old and still white. There is room at the end of the bar for one more, and the wood is worn pale there, where a hand has rested on it every day.

count.speaker: The cords on the lodge gate
count.text: Seventy-one. You count again and get seventy-one. It seems important to have counted.

speaker_name: The bells at the table's foot
notes: A touch at the Brow Long Table's foot (hearthvale.gd long_table).

look.speaker: The bells at the table's foot
look.text: Bronze handles stand up out of a low mound of turf at the foot of the table, green with weather: CADWELL, PENNOCK, TILER, cut into the handles. Beside them, a hole the size of a bell, the turf round it pressed flat by somebody's thumbs.

choices.text: Ring the handles, one after another.

ring.speaker: The bells at the table's foot
ring.text: Three flat notes out of the ground, and then, where the hole is, nothing, and the nothing is somehow the loudest of the four. On the table behind you the crows get up all at once and settle again.

notes: A touch at the Struck Gibbet (hearthvale.gd struck_gibbet): the boards of names the Wardens struck from the Roll.

look.speaker: The name-boards on the gibbets
look.text: Boards hang from the three beams on short chains, black paint on white, each with a name and a stroke through it, turning a little in the wind. The oldest are bare wood, the weather has had them. Some you can read: WAT STONECART, struck. CADELL BROOK, struck. HOB LARKBOURNE, struck, the letters cut deep, as if the painter had been angry. On the middle beam a new board hangs whole: RYN LARKBOURNE, and no stroke through it.

read.speaker: The name-boards on the gibbets
read.text: You read them one by one. It takes some time; there are a great many. When you stop, the crows on the beams are all looking at you, and the wind has dropped, and one of the boards has stopped turning, as if it wanted to hear the end.

notes: A touch at the telling-bench of the Rookdown Bee-Garth (hearthvale.gd bee_garth). Tibby Wax asks a stranger to tell the bees about the grey on the green.

look.speaker: The skeps
look.text: A bench by the garth gate, worn smooth, and before it a niche in the wall with a straw skep in it, humming. Rookdown tells its bees everything, from here, quietly, so they stay.

choices.text: Tell them the grey on the green has reached the well.
Tell them you passed this way.

grey.speaker: The skeps
grey.text: You tell them, low, the way the Vale does. The humming stops. For a long moment the garth is quite silent and you can hear the rooks down in Rookdown. Then, from every niche in the wall at once, the humming comes back, a little lower than before, and steady.

passed.speaker: The skeps
passed.text: A stranger, come up the down and gone again. The humming does not change. They have been told stranger things.

notes: A touch between the Hushwatch stones (hearthvale.gd hushwatch): the custom is to say one name out loud before turning back.

look.speaker: Between the Hushwatch stones
look.text: Between the three stones the Hush lies below you to the south, grey as slate, very flat, very still, and so quiet that you can hear your own blood. The Vale's custom is to say one name out loud here before turning back.

choices.text: Say the name of somebody you have lost.

lost.speaker: Between the Hushwatch stones
lost.text: You say it. The Hush takes it the way deep water takes a stone, without a sound. You feel lighter, going home, and you could not say why.

own.speaker: Between the Hushwatch stones
own.text: You say it, and for a moment the stones seem to lean in to hear it, as the Vale leans in to hear a name on Naming Day. It is a good name. Somebody should keep it. Somebody will.

larkstead.speaker: Between the Hushwatch stones
larkstead.text: You say it. Nothing happens, for as long as it takes to be sure nothing is going to happen. Then, from very far down under the Brow, under the wind, a few bars of singing, four voices, and a laugh that might be a child's.

notes: A touch at the foot of Briarfoot Watch (hearthvale.gd briarfoot_watch).

look.speaker: The tally-board at Briarfoot
look.text: A black board nailed to the tower's foot, chalked in two neat hands: the gate shut, the thorn across it, the grey a stride and a half off the Southgate Stone, then a stride. Low down, where a person would chalk if they were kneeling, a third hand: IT IS NOT COMING TO THE STONE. IT IS COMING TO THE TOWER. ASK WHO IS ON THE TERRACES AT MIDNIGHT.

choices.text: Chalk your own line under it.

chalk.speaker: The tally-board at Briarfoot
chalk.text: You chalk what you have seen on the road here, plainly, the way the Wardens do, and put your initial after it. It looks very small beside the third hand.

notes: A touch before the Listener's Shieling (hearthvale.gd listeners_shieling): sit still and listen.

look.speaker: The Brow, listening
look.text: You sit on the turf by the writing table with your back to the hut and face the Hush. The wind comes up the cliff in long breaths. Between the breaths there is a stillness so complete you can hear the ink drying in the Listener's book.

choices.text: Wait for the wind to drop.

wait.speaker: The Brow, listening
wait.text: It drops. For a few bars, under nothing, from nowhere, four voices, low: *we kept the note, we kept the note*. Then the wind again, and a lark going up off the down as if it had been startled by something it had heard too.

speaker_name: The shift board at Knappers' Deep
notes: A touch on the headframe's leg at Knappers' Deep (hearthvale.gd knappers_deep).

look.speaker: The shift board at Knappers' Deep
look.text: A board of tarred elm nailed to the headframe's leg, NIGHT SHIFT painted across the top. Under it seven names in chalk, the strokes gone soft and furred with eleven winters: Hal Cresswell. Toby Cresswell. Wat Ashdown. Dunn. Little Dunn. Edric Tallow. Pip. And under them, smaller, A. KNAPPER, OVERMAN. The chalk has been gone over again, recently, every letter, by somebody who did not want them to fade.

choices.text: Put your ear to the leg.

listen.speaker: The shift board at Knappers' Deep
listen.text: The timber carries the sound up from a long way under the down. Knocking, slow and even, iron on chalk: seven, a pause, and one.

notes: A touch at the Hum Stone's foot (hearthvale.gd hum_stone).

look.speaker: The Hum Stone
look.text: The stone is warmer than the air, and smoother than anything left out on the Brow ought to be, as if it were poured. Under your palm it is humming: not loud, not a sound at all until you put your hand on it, and then it is in your teeth. The note is low, and steady, and very slightly flat, and somewhere in it, a long way down, there is a second note, much fainter, that might be a voice.

keep.speaker: The Hum Stone
keep.text: The longer you listen the surer you are that the second note is a voice, and that it is not singing. It is saying a name over and over, the way you say a name so as not to forget it. You almost have it. Then the wind gets up off the Hush and you have lost it.

notes: A touch at the bellwright's frame by the Hum Stone (hearthvale.gd hum_stone).

look.speaker: Godwin Merrow's tuning bells
look.text: Five hand-bells on a beam, each with a strip of paper tied to its handle in a small careful hand: TOLL. MERROW. CRESSWELL. ASHDOWN. THE STONE. The last one has been filed and filed at the lip until the bronze is thin there.

choices.text: Strike the one marked THE STONE.

strike.speaker: Godwin Merrow's tuning bells
strike.text: It rings, and the Hum Stone answers it, the two notes leaning on each other until they are one note, and for a breath the whole Brow is in tune. Then the stone's note sags, flat, the way a voice does when it is tired, and the little bell is left ringing on its own.

speaker_name: The cist in Orm's Long Barrow
notes: A touch at Orm's Long Barrow (hearthvale.gd orms_long_barrow).

look.speaker: The cist in Orm's Long Barrow
look.text: The robbers dug a trench across the barrow's back down to the cist and lifted its capstones off one by one, and stacked them on the grass as neatly as a mason would. The cist is a box of four sarsens on edge, deep enough to stand in. It is empty but for the chalk floor, swept, and the marks in the chalk where something long lay for two thousand years and is not lying there now.

choices.text: Climb down the ladder and look closer.

closer.speaker: The cist in Orm's Long Barrow
closer.text: Scratched into the inside of the end stone, small and very old, are rows of marks like a tally, and under them in a newer hand, in Valish, two names you know from Tamwick: a Coppin and a Graft. Somebody has been keeping a count down here, and Tamwick is on it twice. The robbers did not take anything. You begin to see why they stacked the stones so carefully: so they could put them back.

speaker_name: The new wall in Tallow Barrow
notes: A touch at Tallow Barrow's walled-up entrance (hearthvale.gd tallow_barrow).

look.speaker: The new wall in Tallow Barrow
look.text: The way into the barrow is walled up with knapped flint, coursed and pointed with lime by somebody who knew how, and every flint faces outward, the way you build a wall to keep a thing in rather than out. There is a gap in it this spring the height and width of a door. The flints round the gap are warm under your hand, like a hearth-back in the morning, and the air coming out of the dark smells of tallow and of something being kept.

listen.speaker: The new wall in Tallow Barrow
listen.text: Inside, a long way in, someone is laying flint: the tap of a hammer-stone, a pause, the scrape of lime on a trowel. The work is slow and very patient. It is, you realise, the gap that is being walled up again, from the inside, and the someone has nearly finished.

speaker_name: The nine bells at the Warden Barrow
notes: A touch at the Warden Barrow's bells (hearthvale.gd warden_barrow).

look.speaker: The nine bells at the Warden Barrow
look.text: Nine hand-bells, eight on oak posts round the kerb and the ninth hung from the lintel over the barrow's door, each with a name burned into its post-arm in the Wardens' plain capitals. The youngest at the Rest rings them every Tollday, one after another, round the kerb from left to right. This year the youngest has not come.

choices.text: Ring them round, left to right.

ring.speaker: The nine bells at the Warden Barrow
ring.text: You ring them round, one after another. Eight notes go out over the down. When you ring the ninth, over the door, it is answered from inside the barrow by a tenth bell, smaller, a little flat, rung once by a hand that knows how. Then nothing.

speaker_name: The bell on the Pinfold gate
notes: A touch at the Pinfold's gate (hearthvale.gd the_pinfold).

look.speaker: The bell on the Pinfold gate
look.text: A hand-bell on an arm off the gate-post, its rope worn grey. You ring it to say you have come to pay the penny and take your beast home. Inside the pound the strays look up.

ring.speaker: The bell on the Pinfold gate
ring.text: It rings, and every beast in the pound turns to the gate, and then one of them, a ewe with no mark on her, walks to the gate and stands there as if she had been rung for. Nobody in the Vale owns her. Every morning there is one more of her.

speaker_name: The hayward's board at the Pinfold
notes: A touch at the Pinfold's board (hearthvale.gd the_pinfold).

look.speaker: The hayward's board at the Pinfold
look.text: PINFOLD. STRAYS PENNED BY THE HAYWARD OF MERROWBY. ONE PENNY THE HEAD, PAID AT THE GATE. RING AND WAIT. Under it in chalk, the week's count in the hayward's tally-strokes, and under those, in another hand, in the same chalk, a stroke too many every day.

count.speaker: The hayward's board at the Pinfold
count.text: Five beasts penned on Monday and six strokes; three on Tuesday and four; none on Wednesday, and one. The extra stroke is always the last, a little shorter than the others, as if made by someone with smaller hands.

speaker_name: The plough in the Last Field
notes: A touch at the Last Field's plough (hearthvale.gd the_last_field).

look.speaker: The plough in the Last Field
look.text: The Southcotes left their plough standing in the middle furrow the year the grey reached it, its share in the ground and its handles up, and walked to Rookdown without looking back. Its timber has gone silver. The furrow behind it is brown and the furrow in front of it is grey, and the line between is as clean as a knife.

choices.text: Look at the furrow in front of it.

furrow.speaker: The plough in the Last Field
furrow.text: There is a fresh furrow in front of the plough that was not there in the spring, a single one, cut clean into the grey, with the grey turned up on its lip like ash. The share is bright where it went in. Nobody has been near it. The Southcotes' dead, Rookdown says, are still ploughing their last field, and they have got a furrow further.

notes: A touch at the Cliff Graves' turned headstone (hearthvale.gd cliff_graves).

look.speaker: The turned headstone
look.text: Every headstone in the row faces the Hush, so the drowned will see it coming if it comes back for the rest of Rookdown. This one faces inland. The turf at its foot is not disturbed. It has been turned round the way a sleeper turns over.

read.speaker: The turned headstone
read.text: IDE ROOKWELL. TAKEN BY THE WATER. Under it, cut later and not so well: SHE KEPT THE FIRE. The stone is facing up the Brow, toward the Cliff Hearth, where a Rookwell still keeps the fire lit on the nights the other houses forget.

speaker_name: The doorstone of the Chalk Cell
notes: A touch at the Chalk Cell's doorstone (hearthvale.gd chalk_cell).

look.speaker: The doorstone of the Chalk Cell
look.text: A flat stone by the cell's door, worn hollow in the middle by forty years of loaves set down on it. The Vale brought the hermit her bread here and never knocked. She died thirty years ago. There is a loaf on it now, this morning's, and the one that was left yesterday has gone.

choices.text: Leave a little of your own food.

leave.speaker: The doorstone of the Chalk Cell
leave.text: You set it down beside the loaf. When you look back from the end of the flags the door is a hand wider open than it was, and from the dark inside, somebody says thank you in a Sedgish accent, very quietly, the way you say it to someone you do not want to come in.

notes: A touch at the Roll Stone (hearthvale.gd roll_stone).

look.speaker: The Roll Stone
look.text: Four names cut down the stone's face in the Wardens' plain capitals, each with a stroke through it, cut later and deeper: MULLBOURNE. HAREWELL. LARKSTEAD. GOSFORD. Under them the stone is dressed smooth for a hand's depth more, and left bare. The Wardens walk out from the Rest on Tollday and read the four names aloud to it, struck as they are, because a name read aloud is a name kept.

choices.text: Look at the bare stone under them.

read.speaker: The Roll Stone
read.text: You read them aloud, the four of them, and the wind drops while you do it, and gets up again after. It is a small thing to do. Nobody else is on the down to hear it. It seems to be enough.

bare.speaker: The Roll Stone
bare.text: The bare stone under the four names has been dressed ready for a fifth. Somebody has scratched in it, very lightly, with the point of a knife, the first stroke of a letter, and stopped.

notes: A touch at the Hare Stone (hearthvale.gd hare_stone).

look.speaker: The Hare Stone
look.text: On the Vale side of the stone a hare is cut, sitting up with its ears back, and on the Wold side an oak leaf; both have been rubbed so smooth and pale by hands that they shine. Every carter going over into the Wold puts a hand on the hare for luck, and every one coming back puts a hand on the leaf for leave. Nobody remembers who said to.

choices.text: Put your hand on the hare.
Put your hand on the leaf.

hare.speaker: The Hare Stone
hare.text: The stone is warm where the hare is, warmer than the sun would make it, the way a seat is warm when somebody has just got up. You feel lucky, or at least watched over by somebody who does not mind you.

leaf.speaker: The Hare Stone
leaf.text: The leaf is cool and a little damp, like the underside of a real one. Somewhere in the oaks over the boundary a jay calls once, which the carters say is leave given.

notes: A touch at the Weighing Stone (hearthvale.gd the_weighing_stone).

look.speaker: The weighing-beam
look.text: The carters' beam: an oak balk on an iron pin, a hook and chains at the short end for the load and a stone weight on the long end, slid along until the beam hangs level. The notches along it are the weights in hundredweight and quarters, and beside the notches carters have cut their marks, one for every load weighed fair, two hundred years of them.

weigh.speaker: The weighing-beam
weigh.text: You hang off the hook by your hands while the stone weight finds its notch. A hundredweight and a half and a quarter, near enough. Somebody has cut a small hare beside the notch where you hang, and under it, very old, YOU WEIGH WHAT YOU CARRY.

notes: A touch at the Naming Stone (hearthvale.gd the_naming_stone).

look.speaker: The Naming Stone
look.text: At a child's height on the stone's face the dressing is worn into shallow hollows, the shape of small hands, laid over each other a thousand times. On Naming Day each child of the downs stands on the step and puts a hand flat on the stone, and the whole down says the child's name back to it three times, so that the stone has heard it and will not forget.

choices.text: Put your hand there and say your own name.

name.speaker: The Naming Stone
name.text: Your hand is too big for the hollows; it covers four of them. You say your name, and nobody on the down says it back. Then, a long way off, from the direction of Bramcombe, somebody calls it, once, as if they had heard you and were answering. It might have been a lark.

notes: A touch at the lamp niche in Wake Barrow's forecourt (hearthvale.gd wake_barrow).

look.speaker: The forecourt lamp
look.text: A horn lantern in a box of four slabs and a capstone, the slabs black with two hundred years of soot on the inside. The wick has been trimmed this morning and the oil is full. Scratched on the capstone, over and over in different hands, the same three strokes and a name: EBBA.

choices.text: Hold your hand over the lamp.

hand.speaker: The forecourt lamp
hand.text: The flame leans toward the barrow, as if there were a draught going in. There is no wind. When you take your hand away it leans further.

notes: A touch at the first coffin-rest on the way up to Wake Barrow (hearthvale.gd wake_barrow).

look.speaker: The coffin-rest
look.text: A flat stone at knee height, worn into two shallow troughs by the feet of coffins set down on it, and at its head a cup worn into the stone where the bearers put a coin for the barrow-wife. There is a coin in the cup, a new one, and three more under the grass beside it, old.

choices.text: Leave a coin in the cup.

coin.speaker: The coffin-rest
coin.text: It rings on the stone. Up at the barrow, the lamp in the forecourt flares for a moment, as though somebody had opened a door.

notes: A touch at the Letter-Cote's letter-table (hearthvale.gd letter_cote): a dove sent for three marks to one of the places the cote knows comes back having seen it, and the place is found (discover); the dove sent to Harewell comes back with a letter.

look.speaker: The cote-wife's letter-table
look.text: A trestle by the cote door: a slate of the Vale's villages and places with a bird-basket under each name, strips of birch-bark, a pot of soot-ink, and a chalked notice: A DOVE, THREE MARKS. IT GOES WHERE IT'S SENT AND COMES HOME WITH WHAT IT SAW.

choices.text: Send a dove to the old press on the East Downs. (3 marks)
Send a dove to the crown of Hound Down. (3 marks)
Send a dove to the chandlers on the West Downs. (3 marks)
Send a dove to the figure-cutters over the Tamwick road. (3 marks)
Send a dove to Harewell. (3 marks)

knap.speaker: The cote-wife's letter-table
knap.text: The dove goes up out of the lantern and east, and comes back before you have counted a hundred, with apple blossom stuck in its feathers, in the wrong month, and a smell of cider. Wassail Knap: the old press over Hazelcombe, a long roof, a beam like a whole tree, and an orchard round it.

moot.speaker: The cote-wife's letter-table
moot.text: The dove goes up out of the lantern and south-east, and comes back with a straw in its beak and its feathers on end. The crown of Hound Down: forty figures in ranks on the skyline, all facing the same way, and an old man walking along them.

wheel.speaker: The cote-wife's letter-table
wheel.text: The dove goes up and west and comes back smelling of hot tallow, with a smear of wax on one foot. The West Downs: a mast with a wheel at its head as wide as a cottage, hung with candles, turning.

harewell.speaker: The cote-wife's letter-table
harewell.text: The dove goes up out of the lantern and does not go anywhere you can follow: it goes into the haze over the West Downs and is simply not there. You wait. The cote-wife's birds come and go. Then it drops onto the table beside your hand, cold and wet with fog, with a roll of birch-bark on its leg.

figure.speaker: The cote-wife's letter-table
figure.text: The dove goes east and comes back with chalk dust on its breast. The down over the Tamwick road: a woman cut white into the turf, thirty paces tall, holding up a candle, with no face. The cote-wife watches it come in and does not say anything.

notes: A touch at the box of answered letters by the Letter-Cote's door (hearthvale.gd letter_cote).

look.speaker: The answered letters
look.text: A painted box with a slot in the lid, MULLBOURNE HAREWELL LARKSTEAD GOSFORD on its four sides in four colours. Inside, a sheaf of birch-bark rolls, each no bigger than a finger, each tied with the cote's green thread to show it came back. The top one is unrolled and weighted with a pebble.

read.speaker: The answered letters
read.text: *Larkstead, in a man's hand, careful:* Mistress Cotter. We had your letter. We are not lost; we are here; it is the roads that went. Tell Harewell their barley is not better than ours. -- *Under it, in the cote-wife's hand:* Told them. W.C.

notes: A touch at the Candle-Wheel's tallow vat (hearthvale.gd candle_wheel): for five marks a candle is dipped for a name and set on the shelf. Each name once; the names grow with the quests done (being named holds: the Candle).

look.speaker: The tallow vat
look.text: The vat steams under the wheel's rim, the tallow in it the colour of new cream. A slate leans on the hearth: A CANDLE DIPPED FOR A NAME, FIVE MARKS. THE DIPPERS KEEP IT LIT. Under it, smaller: SAY THE NAME ALOUD WHILE IT IS DIPPED, OR IT IS ONLY A CANDLE.

choices.text: Have one dipped for your own name. (5 marks)
Have one dipped for the four villages off the Roll Stone. (5 marks)
Have one dipped for Ebba Crowle, the barrow-wife. (5 marks)
Have one dipped for Hob Applegarth, the last Wassail King. (5 marks)
Have one dipped for the night shift at Knappers' Deep. (5 marks)

own.speaker: The tallow vat
own.text: The wick goes down into the tallow thirty times, and you say your name thirty times, and by the end it sounds like somebody else's, a name the Vale has always had. The candle goes on the shelf among the Roll's. Somebody will light it tonight who has never met you.

villages.speaker: The tallow vat
villages.text: Four wicks on one rod. Mullbourne, Harewell, Larkstead, Gosford, thirty times each. On the shelf they lean together, the four of them, the way people stand who have walked a long way in fog.

ebba.speaker: The tallow vat
ebba.text: Ebba Crowle, barrow-wife, thirty times. The candle comes out of the last dip with a thread of soot down it from nowhere, three short strokes, like a tally.

hob.speaker: The tallow vat
hob.text: Hob Applegarth, thirty times. The candle smells of apples when it is lit, and it burns down twice as fast as the others and has to be dipped again, which seems right.

shift.speaker: The tallow vat
shift.text: Seven wicks on one rod and one on its own: the shift, and the overman. Thirty dips. When they are set on the shelf the flames gutter all together, seven and then one, and then burn straight.

notes: A touch at the Candle-Wheel's candle-house (hearthvale.gd candle_wheel).

look.speaker: The Roll candles
look.text: Three shelves of candles burning in the open-fronted shed, each with a name chalked on the plank under it in the Dippers' plain capitals: wardens of the Rest, back and back, hundreds of them, every flame upright. One space in the middle shelf is dark.

dark.speaker: The Roll candles
dark.text: A candle stub, cold, its wick pinched black. The plank under it has been scraped bare in a smear the width of a thumb. If you look at it slant, against the light of the others, there is the ghost of a capital A, and a long stroke.

amis.speaker: The Roll candles
amis.text: AMIS HALE, BRIARFOOT, chalked fresh. Her flame leans south, toward the Briar, steadily, the way a Warden on a gate leans toward the gate.

speaker_name: The end of the third rank
notes: The touch TheOddOne at the Scarecrow Moot: looking it in the face wakes the forty-first (encounters/pois_hearthvale.json rises_when).

look.speaker: The end of the third rank
look.text: A scarecrow like the others, in a good grey coat too good for a field, its hat pulled low. The straw at its cuffs is fresh. There is clay on its boots, wet, though it has not rained in a week. You lift the brim. -- Under it there is no sack. There is a face as grey as the down, with earth in its eyes, and it has been looking at Merrowby all summer the way the others do. Now it looks at you.

speaker_name: A scarecrow in a hurdle-maker's smock
notes: A touch on a scarecrow at the Scarecrow Moot (hearthvale.gd scarecrow_moot).

look.speaker: A scarecrow in a hurdle-maker's smock
look.text: A long smock bleached nearly white, the pockets torn by years of hazel wands. HURDLEGATE is burnt into the crossbar in a farmer's letters, and under it a tally of years: seven strokes, and twenty more since. When the wind takes the sleeves they point down the Vale toward the Hurdlegate fields.

choices.text: Say the farm's name to it.

say.speaker: A scarecrow in a hurdle-maker's smock
say.text: "Hurdlegate." The rook on its arm shifts its feet and settles, and the sleeves stop turning in the wind, all at once, pointing home.

speaker_name: A scarecrow with a bell on its arm
notes: A touch on a scarecrow at the Scarecrow Moot (hearthvale.gd scarecrow_moot).

look.speaker: A scarecrow with a bell on its arm
look.text: A red coat gone the brown of old blood, a sheep-bell tied to the right arm with its clapper wrapped in wool so it will not ring. COLDHARBOUR on the crossbar. Its hat is gone; somebody has taken it, and put a wreath of plaited straw on the sack instead, carefully.

bell.speaker: A scarecrow with a bell on its arm
bell.text: You unwind the wool and the bell rings once in the wind. Every rook on the Moot looks at you. You wrap it again. They look away.

notes: A touch at the Scarecrow Moot's tally-post (hearthvale.gd scarecrow_moot).

look.speaker: The reeve's tally
look.text: A board on a post, chalked in a slow old hand: forty farms, a line each, and the man or woman who carried each scarecrow up. HURDLEGATE, by Ned. COLDHARBOUR, by the widow. ASHWAY, by Rab's father ... At the foot: FORTY. A.S. -- And under that, in the same hand but shakier, done since: 41?

count.speaker: The reeve's tally
count.text: You walk the ranks and count. Forty-one. You count again from the other end and get forty-one again. The one at the end of the third rank is the only one without a farm burnt on its cross.

notes: A touch at the cellar grates of Wassail Knap's press-house (hearthvale.gd wassail_knap).

look.speaker: The cellar grate
look.text: An iron grate in the turf along the press-house's front, the bars worn bright by forty years of somebody's hands. Cold air comes up through it, and the smell of cider, and of apples gone to vinegar.

night.speaker: The cellar grate
night.text: Singing. A lot of voices, a long way down, the old wassail, every verse of it, and a fiddle under it, and one voice louder than all the rest, a big kind laughing voice, a beat ahead, leading. It does not stop for breath.

day.speaker: The cellar grate
day.text: Nothing at first. Then, very far down, somebody humming the wassail to themselves, the way you hum when you are waiting for the others to wake up.

quiet.speaker: The cellar grate
quiet.text: Nothing. A drip, a long way down, and the cellar breathing out cold. It is the quiet of a house after a party, when everybody has gone home.

notes: A touch at the wassail bowl in Wassail Knap's forecourt (hearthvale.gd wassail_knap).

look.speaker: The wassail bowl
look.text: A great bowl turned from one piece of apple-wood, wide as a cartwheel, on a trestle under the Wassail Tree. It is full to the brim with cider, fresh and cloudy, and a crust of toast floats in it. Nobody from Hazelcombe has filled it. There are rings on the trestle where it has been lifted and set down, lifted and set down.

drink.speaker: The wassail bowl
drink.text: It is the best cider you have ever had. For a moment the singing is right there, under your feet, and you know all the words, and you have taken a step toward the cellar-head before you know it. You put the bowl down. Your hands want to pick it up again.

notes: The touch at Tamwick Troy's maypole (hearthvale.gd tamwick_troy): reached only by walking the rings. A name said there.

look.speaker: The heart of the Troy
look.text: The maypole stands in the middle of the last ring, hung with ribbons, a name stitched on every one in Maudie Twelvetrees' small red stitches. They talk to each other in the wind. One, low down, is plain.

choices.text: Say your own name, and have a ribbon tied for it.
Say the four quiet villages' names.

own.speaker: The heart of the Troy
own.text: You say it, at the heart, after five rings of hawthorn and all the way round the world. It sounds like it did when you were small. On the way out Maudie Twelvetrees has the ribbon ready, your name in red stitches, and ties it at your throat instead of on the pole. "You'll want it with you," she says. "Where you're going."

villages.speaker: The heart of the Troy
villages.text: Mullbourne. Harewell. Larkstead. Gosford. The ribbons all lift together in a wind you do not feel, and settle.

amis.speaker: The heart of the Troy
amis.text: Amis Hale, Warden, Briarfoot. A ribbon you had not noticed, high up, green and grey, the Wardens' colours, turns in the wind to face south.

plain.speaker: The heart of the Troy
plain.text: It is warm, as if somebody had just let go of it. For a moment you nearly know a name, the way you nearly know a word, and then it is gone and the ribbon is only a ribbon.

notes: A touch at Tamwick Troy's gate (hearthvale.gd tamwick_troy).

look.speaker: The Troy-stone
look.text: A sarsen at the gate, cut in old letters worn soft: IN ALL THE WAY ROUND. OUT ALL THE WAY ROUND. SAY IT AT THE HEART. And under it, newer: NO STEPPING THROUGH. M.T.

notes: A touch at the Unfinished Figure's head (hearthvale.gd unfinished_figure): choosing her face cuts it, and the builder draws it cut (the flags figure_face_cut / figure_face_from_letter).

look.speaker: Where her face should be
look.text: A ring of pegs on the down's face and string between them, the size of a cart-shed: her head. Inside it the turf is laid back down in squares, neat, the cut lines still showing like the seams in a quilt. Col Whitcut's iron is stuck in the turf beside it.

choices.text: Read the cutters the Harewell child's letter, and have them cut her from that.
Tell the cutters to give her a face of the Vale's own, any woman's, and cut it deep.

letter.speaker: Where her face should be
letter.text: You read it out on the down: the barley, the well, the fog that goes back a bit when a letter comes. Col Whitcut listens with his iron in his hands. "Round," he says. "A round careful face. Somebody's mother." They cut it before dark. In the morning the turf has not come back, and there is a dove on her candle.

any.speaker: Where her face should be
any.text: "Any woman's," Col Whitcut says, and looks at the Vale a long time, and cuts his own mother's, he says, from memory. It is a good face. In the morning half the turf is back on it, laid neat, and they cut it again, deeper, and it stays.

cut.speaker: Where her face should be
cut.text: Her face is cut white into the down, two eyes and a mouth and the round of her cheek, looking down at the Tamwick road. From up close it is only trenches in chalk. From the road, people stop.

notes: A touch at the Unfinished Figure's cutters' yard (hearthvale.gd unfinished_figure).

look.speaker: The cutters' turfing irons
look.text: Turfing irons and a spade stuck in the chalk, a heap of lifted turves, and a slate: TURVES TODAY, with a row of strokes. The cutters could do with another back.

choices.text: Lift a row of turves along her hem.

cut.speaker: The cutters' turfing irons
cut.text: You cut along the string, lift the turf in squares and stack it, and scrape the chalk under it clean and white. It is heavy and slow and by the end of the row your back is gone. Col Whitcut chalks your strokes on the slate with his own and pays you a cutter's day, twelve marks, and says you cut crooked.

notes: The touch at the Witness Elms' stump (hearthvale.gd witness_elms): a bright thing (two marks) and the rooks show a place you have not found.

look.speaker: The offering stump
look.text: An elm bole sawn waist-high, its top heaped with buttons, buckles, pins, a spoon, the brass gone dark under the bright. Two hundred rooks in the elms over it go quiet as you come up, and every one of them is looking at your hands.

choices.text: Leave a bright coin, and ask what they've seen in the dells. (2 marks)
Leave a bright coin, and ask what they've seen in the chalk. (2 marks)
Leave a bright coin, and ask what they've seen under Hound Down. (2 marks)
Leave a bright coin, and ask what they've seen at the grey's edge. (2 marks)

dell.speaker: The offering stump
dell.text: A rook drops onto the stump, takes the coin in its beak, and goes west and down, low over the hedges, and the whole rookery turns to watch it go into a fold of the land full of foxgloves, where nobody would think to look.

cell.speaker: The offering stump
cell.text: The coin goes, and a rook goes with it, north and west to a white face of chalk with a door cut in it and a loaf on the doorstone. It circles there three times so you can mark it.

holes.speaker: The offering stump
holes.text: The rook takes the coin and goes down Hound Down's flank, and drops, and does not come up for a long time, into holes in the turf you would have walked straight past: the deneholes.

grey.speaker: The offering stump
grey.text: The rook takes the coin and will not go. Another goes instead, south-east, and stops in the air over a place where the green goes grey, and hangs there, and comes back with no coin and its feathers dull.

notes: A touch in the Great Barn's wagon porch (hearthvale.gd great_barn).

look.speaker: The tithe-board
look.text: A board in the porch, the farms of the East Downs painted down it and a peg-hole for every sheaf owed. The pegs are all in, fifty years in, the last harvest paid to the sheaf. Somebody has pushed a stalk of green barley into the empty peg-hole at the bottom, under SOUTHGATE, where the reeve's own tithe was owed. It is fresh.
